extracted.intended_audience: college students and citizens seeking a general survey of the American political system
extracted.subtask_description: A college-level textbook treatment of American government and politics, tracing historical foundations (colonial origins, Revolution) and explaining institutional structures and powers at colonial, state, and federal levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutions rooted in colonial experience
rubrics_metrics.description: American government did not originate in abstract theory but in the actual experience gained by generations of English colonists in managing their own political affairs; many institutions and names (Senate, House, President) and clauses were taken from state experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that continuity from colonial and state institutions shaped the federal Constitution; use historical origins to understand why specific features (two senators per state, electoral system, checks and balances) exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of colonial executive authority (royal, charter, proprietary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Colonies had different executive structures: royal colonies with governor appointed by the king; charter colonies (e.g., Connecticut, Rhode Island) with locally-authorized governor and less executive independence; proprietary colonies (Maryland, Pennsylvania, Delaware) where proprietors held quasi-feudal authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish how appointment, powers, and relations with assemblies varied by type; use this taxonomy to explain later state-level attitudes toward executive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governor's prerogatives in royal colonies
rubrics_metrics.description: The royal governor was the king's deputy with broad powers: supervised enforcement of laws, appointed important civil officers (often with council advice), removed officials for cause, acted as chancellor (head of highest court), granted pardons and reprieves, commander-in-chief of colonial forces, and exercised nomination/dissolution/adjournment of assemblies and veto of laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows why early state constitution-makers feared executive authority and why many early state constitutions emphasized legislative supremacy and weak governors; examples include appointment of sheriffs affecting elections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governor's constraints via instructions, assemblies, and purse
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite broad legal prerogatives, royal governors were constrained by instructions from home, assemblies' control over money grants, appeals to the Board of Trade or king in council, and the growing claims of councils over patronage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these political and financial levers to explain frequent assembly victories over governors in colonial disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charter-colony executive structure (Massachusetts exception noted)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Massachusetts under its charter the governor could adjourn/prorogue/dissolve the assembly but could not appoint the council or choose civil officers without the council's consent; this division often produced conflict and contributed to Massachusetts leading resistance to royal authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterize Massachusetts as having a mixed executive that limited unilateral gubernatorial appointment power, altering the balance with the legislature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connecticut and Rhode Island executive form (assembly-elected governor)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Rhode Island and Connecticut the governor was elected annually by a general assembly composed of governor, assistants, and representatives; the governor functioned largely in cooperation with assistants/councillors and lacked veto power; executive and legislative powers were not sharply separated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These colonies kept executive authority closely tied to popular assemblies, influencing later preferences for limited executive power and legislative primacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proprietary-colony executive/patronage system
rubrics_metrics.description: In proprietary colonies the proprietor (a 'petty king') held titles to land and substantial sovereign rights; when absentee, a lieutenant-governor acted as agent. Governors had claims to veto and broad patronage, though assemblies often contested these powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples from Pennsylvania and Maryland to show how proprietary rights affected governance and legislative resistance over executive appointments and revenue sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upper house (council) selection and role
rubrics_metrics.description: In royal colonies the council (upper house) was nominated by the king via governor; in proprietary colonies chosen by the proprietor; in New England (Mass., Conn., R.I.) the upper house (assistants/councillors) was often chosen by the general assembly and thus less independent. Councils exercised executive/judicial functions and advised governors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Councils merged with executive authority where appointed, forming aristocratic bodies aligned with governors; where elected, they tended to merge with legislatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative (assembly) powers and control over executive
rubrics_metrics.description: Assemblies asserted broad authority over domestic concerns, especially taxation, and used control of salaries and money grants to restrain governors; legislatures had general powers to make laws for the welfare of the province (so long as not repugnant to English law).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes assemblies' practical leverage (purse-strings) as the main check on executive power in colonial practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal limitations on colonial legislative authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Colonial legislatures faced legal limits: governors' veto power (in many colonies), requirement in most colonies that laws be sent to England for royal approval, and Parliamentary statutes asserting Parliament's supremacy to make laws binding the colonies in all cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites that some colonial laws could be declared null and void if repugnant to English laws; this background explains colonial legal disputes and later acceptance of judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property qualifications for suffrage (colonial)
rubrics_metrics.description: Voting was not universal; colonies imposed property qualifications: e.g., New York — freeholders of lands/tenements worth 40 pounds (with city exceptions), Virginia — freeholder of specified acreage or house ownership, Massachusetts — freeholder of estate of specified value, Pennsylvania — freeholders of 50 acres or wealth of 50 pounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantitative estimates illustrate that only a small fraction (varying by colony) of adult males could vote; explain low colonial turnout and its causes (property, communication, district size, lack of party organization).

rubrics_metrics.name: Property and religious qualifications for legislative membership
rubrics_metrics.description: Many colonies required members of legislatures to meet substantial property qualifications (examples: South Carolina — 500 acres and 10 slaves or £1000 worth; New Jersey — 1000 acres; Georgia — 500 acres) and often imposed religious tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these membership requirements to explain elite composition of colonial legislatures and later democratic reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation by territorial units rather than equal population
rubrics_metrics.description: Representation was distributed among territorial units (towns, counties, parishes) rather than equal population groups. New England used towns, middle colonies used counties, and southern colonies used parishes; equal representation principle was not accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains malapportionment and the historical roots of unequal representation practices in later state/federal arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colonial judicial structure and appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: Colonial courts comprised justices of the peace (local magistrates handling small civil/penal matters), county courts (criminal jurisdiction under capital cases and certain civil amounts), and a high court (colony's supreme court, sometimes governor+ council or appointed judges); appeals lay to English higher authorities (e.g., king in council).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes roles of chancellor/governor in provincial high courts and the channel of appeals to England; shows continuity with English judicial traditions and foundations for judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early exercise of judicial power to invalidate laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Many state courts had already exercised the power to declare laws invalid on constitutional grounds prior to federal practice; early cases illustrate courts declaring colonial/state statutes void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat this as a historical precedent for later judicial review at state and federal levels; references to Thayer and early cases are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governor's influence over elections via appointment of sheriffs
rubrics_metrics.description: Royal governors increased political influence through appointment of local sheriffs, who acted as returning officers at elections, thereby affecting assembly composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as an example of executive leverage over representative bodies and one reason assemblies distrusted governors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical limits to franchise and electoral participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of property qualifications, poor communication, large districts, and absence of party organization, actual voter turnout was low—often only a small fraction (examples: Boston ~3% of population; New York City 1/9 to 1/14 potential voters; rural Pennsylvania ~10% eligible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantitative figures illustrate the limited nature of colonial democracy and why later expansion of suffrage was significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative general power under charters
rubrics_metrics.description: Charters commonly conferred 'full power and authority ... to make, ordain, and establish all manner of wholesome and reasonable orders, laws, statutes, and ordinances' for the good of the province provided they were not repugnant to laws of England.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights the general (not specific) nature of colonial legislative grants and why more concrete constitutional definitions developed post-independence.
